title: Short Stuff: The Mona Lisa
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Mona Lisa. The hosts cover who the sitter is (Lisa Gherardini, also called Lisa del Giocondo, wife of a silk merchant, possibly commissioned to celebrate a birth), Leonardo da Vinci's sfumato technique and lack of hard lines, the painting's background landscape and an Italian research team's proposed real location, the "Mona Lisa effect" of eyes seeming to follow viewers, and the painting's rise to fame after its 1911 theft from the Louvre, including the suspects named, the 28-month recovery, and Vincenzo Peruggia's trial and sentence.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the Mona Lisa
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on the Mona Lisa, note the painting's small size and protective casing, and identify the sitter as Lisa Gherardini del Giocondo, a wealthy silk merchant's wife, possibly commissioned for a birth.

segments.title: Identity of the sitter and the commission
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why experts believe Lisa Gherardini is the sitter, citing a contemporary book and a later margin note, and speculate that her loose clothing and smile suggest pregnancy.

segments.title: Artistry: sfumato and lack of lines
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss da Vinci's sfumato technique, which uses shading to suggest rather than draw lines, and mention a Nova documentary that explains the method.

segments.title: The background landscape and its proposed location
segments.summary: The hosts describe the blended landscape behind the sitter, and mention Italian researchers who proposed a real location in Montefeltro, while noting the claim is still speculative.

segments.title: The Mona Lisa effect
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the so-called Mona Lisa effect, where the eyes seem to follow viewers, note that research found the effect is not actually demonstrated by the painting, and recount how the sitter appears to look past viewers to their right.

segments.title: Theft from the Louvre, recovery, and fame
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the painting was little known until the mid-1800s, then was stolen in August 1911 by a handyman, went missing for 28 months, drew suspects including Picasso and JP Morgan, and was recovered when Vincenzo Peruggia tried to sell it in Florence, leading to an eight-month sentence.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and sign-off for the Short Stuff episode.
